definition.text: A measure of how strongly the quantity people buy responds to a change in its price: the percentage change in quantity for a one percent change in price.

facts.text: An elasticity of −2 means a one percent price rise cuts the quantity demanded by two percent.
If quantity falls 20 tons from 200 tons after the price rises $5 from $100, quantity drops 10% and price rises 5%, giving an elasticity of −2.
Demand is inelastic when the elasticity is below one in absolute value and elastic when it is above one.
Demand is more elastic when close substitutes exist, and less elastic for necessities such as insulin or for broad categories such as food in general.
Elasticity grows with time: after a lasting fuel price rise, more people switch to carpooling or public transport.
For inelastic goods a price rise increases revenue; for elastic goods it lowers revenue, and revenue peaks where elasticity is exactly one.
Elasticity predicts who bears a tax: with perfectly inelastic demand consumers pay all of it, with perfectly elastic demand firms pay all of it.
Alfred Marshall is credited with defining elasticity of demand in his Principles of Economics of 1890.

definition.text: An elasticity measured between two points on a demand curve, using the average of the two prices and the two quantities as the base.

facts.text: It removes the problem that an ordinary elasticity depends on which point is treated as the starting one, and gives an average elasticity over that arc of the curve.
Hugh Dalton introduced it very early on.
Point elasticity instead uses calculus to measure elasticity for a tiny price change at a single point, but needs the demand formula to be known.

title: Supply and demand

definition.text: The basic economic model of how a market sets prices: the price moves until the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer.

facts.text: The idea of supply and demand is the theoretical foundation of modern economics.
The equilibrium is the price and quantity where the demand and supply curves cross.
Under perfect competition supply follows marginal cost: firms produce more as long as the extra cost is below the market price.
Consumers buy another unit as long as its value to them is more than its price, so the demand curve slopes downward.
Augustin Cournot first drew demand curves in 1838, Fleeming Jenkin added supply curves in 1870, and Alfred Marshall popularized both in 1890.
The fourteenth-century scholar Ibn Taymiyyah wrote that when desire for goods rises while availability falls, the price rises.
The model also explains wages: workers supply labour, businesses demand it, and the equilibrium price is the wage rate.
Where a seller or buyer has market power, models such as oligopoly or monopsony fit better.

contested_note: Sraffa questioned the consistency of partial-equilibrium supply curves, and Post-Keynesians argue the model fails to explain prices that firms set by mark-up.

title: Shifts in supply and demand
article: Supply and demand#Changes in market equilibrium

definition.text: Changes in conditions other than a good's own price that move a whole supply or demand curve, and so change the equilibrium price and quantity.

facts.text: A movement along a curve is a 'change in quantity demanded', while a shift of the whole curve is a 'change in demand'.
Demand can rise because of changing tastes, higher incomes, price changes in substitutes and complements, expectations or more buyers; a rise lifts both equilibrium price and quantity.
A cheaper way of growing wheat shifts supply outward, lowering the price and raising the quantity sold.
A rise in raw-material costs shifts supply to the left, so less is offered at every price.
